name: Fruitarian diet
lead: A fruitarian diet is an eating pattern built primarily or entirely on fruit, sometimes with nuts and seeds, and without animal products. It is more restrictive than veganism or raw veganism, and practitioners differ on what counts as fruit and whether anything else is allowed.[5] In looksmaxxing communities it is sometimes discussed as a route to "clean" skin and leanness.

Published research on the diet is limited to individual case reports. These describe a type 1 diabetes patient who adopted the diet for ideological reasons, a case of reversible dementia attributed to a strictly fruitarian diet, and a leukemia patient who combined a mostly fruitarian diet with long periodic fasts.[1][2][3] No clinical trial has tested a fruitarian diet for skin or appearance outcomes.

Dietitians and health organisations cited in encyclopedic summaries advise against long-term fruit-only eating, citing the risk of deficiencies, particularly vitamin B12, and describe it as unsuitable for children and pregnant or nursing women.[5]
infobox: Animal products; often grains and legumes
Vitamin B12, protein, calcium, iron, zinc

paras: Definitions vary. Some followers eat only plant foods that can be gathered without killing the plant, such as fallen fruit, while others allow legumes, dried fruit, honey, olive oil or cooked foods. Some versions inspired by Jain ethics avoid harming any living thing, including plants.[5]

The diet has older roots in naturopathic and "natural living" movements; the Wikipedia article lists a periodical promoting a fruitarian way of life in the 1896-1918 period and a 1961 book advocating fruit as food and medicine.[5]

Nutrition sources note that fruit contains no vitamin B12, so long-term fruitarians would typically need supplements, and that protein, calcium, iron, zinc, vitamin D and essential fatty acids may also fall short. High sugar intake raises concerns for people with diabetes and for dental health.[5]

Case literature illustrates reported consequences. A 2021 report described dementia in a person following a strictly fruitarian diet that was reversible after the diet changed.[2] A 2022 report described how a young man with type 1 diabetes switching to a fruitarian diet changed his glucose control.[3] Case reports cannot show cause and effect.

No controlled studies of fruitarian diets for skin, weight or appearance outcomes were found. The literature consists of case reports, including those on dementia, type 1 diabetes and a leukemia patient who combined a mostly fruitarian diet with periodic fasting.[1][2][3] A 1978 nursing journal piece also discussed the diet.[4]

The idea of eating only fruit for "clean" skin appears in appearance forums as part of a wider interest in detox, raw and plant-only eating. Proponents argue that fruit is water-rich, high in antioxidants and free of processed food. Critics in medical and dietetic literature point to the deficiency and sugar concerns above.[5]

timeline.event: A periodical promotes a fruitarian system of living.[5]
Morris Krok publishes a book advocating fruit as food and medicine.[5]
An actor is hospitalised after following a fruitarian diet for a film role, widely reported.[5]

lore.intro: Fruitarianism is mentioned in appearance communities mainly as an extreme form of clean eating.

claims.claim: Eating only fruit gives clear, glowing skin.
claims.believers: Proponents say that removing processed food, dairy and animal products and eating water-rich fruit leaves skin clearer and brighter.
claims.experts: No published trial has tested this. Nutrition sources describe risks of deficiencies on fruit-only diets.[5]

claims.claim: A fruit-only diet is a safe long-term way to stay lean.
claims.believers: Advocates say fruit is low in fat and calories and that the body is designed to run on it.
claims.experts: Case reports describe nutritional and metabolic problems, including reversible dementia and glucose-control changes in type 1 diabetes.[2][3]

card.summary: Eating only fruit for clean skin: no appearance trials exist, and case reports describe nutritional problems.
card.note: Fruit contains no vitamin B12; dietitians caution against long-term use.

quick.overview:
A fruitarian diet is based mainly or wholly on fruit, sometimes with nuts and seeds. Some people in appearance communities try it hoping for clearer skin and leanness.

No clinical trials have tested it for appearance. The published literature consists of case reports.
quick.mechanism: Followers say removing processed foods and animal products and eating water-rich, antioxidant-containing fruit improves skin. This mechanism has not been tested in studies.
quick.risks: Dietitians cite possible shortfalls of vitamin B12, protein, calcium, iron, zinc and vitamin D, high sugar load, and unsuitability for children and pregnant or nursing women. Case reports include reversible dementia and altered glucose control in type 1 diabetes.
